title: Acceptance sampler and soft-commit scheduler for speculative decode
creator: Aisha Banerjee
description:
Problem: speculative decode (fast-path multi-model handoff) needs a low-cost, robust way to decide when a tentative decode should be accepted versus when to fall back to a full, slower decode. Current probes are expensive to run at scale and tightly coupled to hard thresholds, which causes oscillation and costly rollbacks.

Proposal: implement an 'acceptance sampler' that computes an acceptance score from lightweight signals (early logits similarity, delta entropy, KV-cache hit heuristics, kernel-affinity confidence) and a 'soft-commit scheduler' that performs an ordered sequence of non-destructive commits. Soft-commit allows the runtime to provisionally surface output to the caller while retaining the ability to cleanly rewind to a slower, full decode if acceptance fails later. This reduces wasted work and smooths latency regressions during capacity churn.

Key ideas:
- Acceptance sampler is a statistically calibrated sampler that emits an acceptance probability, not a binary decision. Sampling reduces probe frequency and amortizes cost across similar requests (per-route sampling budgets).
- Soft-commit scheduler stages three commit levels: preview (immediate token stream from fast path, can be retracted), anchored (markers persisted to KV cache for fast rollback), final (hard commit, evicts fallback candidate). The runtime exposes hooks for these stages.
- Kernel-aware scheduling: scheduler considers kernel selection cost (FP16 vs 4-bit quant kernels, batched vs single-threaded kernels) when forming acceptance budgets and deciding whether to spin up a slower model variant or wait for more probes.
- Attention optimizations: use prefix-sparse attention heuristics to reduce cost of candidate probes; for long-context use sliding-window prefilter to focus sampler on high-information tokens.
- Prefill/decode interplay: prefill warms KV caches and provides cheap signals (cache hit rate, last-layer logits entropy) that feed the sampler; scheduler delays hard-commit until prefill-induced confidence reaches configured thresholds.

Goals:
- Reduce full-decode rollbacks by 40% on tail workloads where speculative routes are frequently accepted but occasionally wrong.
- Keep median latency improvement from speculative decode > 15% vs baseline, while keeping 95th percentile regressions < 5% for critical routes.
- Maintain observable, debuggable acceptance metrics per-route and per-kernel to enable safe rollouts.

Why different from current approaches: instead of fixed acceptance thresholds and single-shot probes, we treat acceptance as a sampled probability and use staged, inexpensive commits. This is resilient to distribution shift and makes graceful fallback simpler operationally.
acceptance_criteria: Runtime exposes acceptance_probability metric and per-request decision trace for 100% of speculative requests
Soft-commit API implemented in runtime with three commit states and documented semantics
Experimental rollout shows >=40% reduction in full-decode rollbacks on test traffic (compare A/B)
No >10% increase in GPU utilization for fastest tier when soft-commit is enabled (configurable sampling)
End-to-end tests for rollback correctness and KV cache coherence pass in CI and stress harness
telemetry_requirements: Per-request acceptance_probability, final_accept boolean, and commit_state timeline
Kernel-affinity signal (chosen kernel id, cost estimate) emitted per probe
Prefill signals: KV cache hit rate, prefix entropy, probe latency breakdown
Rollbacks counters tagged by route/model/kernel and reason (confidence, NACK, resource preemption)
Dashboard: acceptance curve by route vs latency/rollback cost and per-kernel cost heatmap
design_notes:
Sampling strategy: start with rate-limited reservoir sampler for 1% base sampling and adaptive boost for routes with high user impact. Acceptance score composition: weighted sum of early-logit-cosine-similarity (to final logits), delta entropy, cache-warmth score, and kernel-confidence. We will train a light-weight linear calibrator (online isotonic/regression) on historical traces to map raw score -> calibrated probability.

Soft-commit semantics: preview stage must be non-destructive (no eviction of fallback candidate). Anchored stage persists minimal state to speed rollback but still keeps alternative available. Final stage performs atomic promotion. Implement idempotent promotion tokens to avoid double-commits in retries.

Kernel integration: introduce a kernel_cost_estimator that returns an estimated ms/token for candidate kernels under current batch-size and sequence-length distribution. Scheduler uses this estimate to prefer probes whose cost is disproportionately low relative to expected acceptance benefit.

Attention adaptations: for long contexts we run a sparse-prefix attention prefilter on the prefill output to derive locality-weighted token importance; sampler focuses probes on tokens with high importance to improve signal quality without full decode cost.

Operational controls: per-customer/per-route sampling budgets, knobs for sampler aggressiveness, per-kernel probe cost caps, and an emergency circuit-breaker to disable speculative fast-paths automatically when rollback rate exceeds threshold.
tradeoffs:
Pros: lower average latency for common cases, fewer wasted full-decodes, and smoother tail behavior via staged commit. Cons: increased system complexity (commit state machine and trace plumbing), slight additional memory footprint to retain alternative decode candidates until final commit, potential transient user-visible retractions in preview stage which product/UX must handle. Calibration errors could bias towards over-accepting; mitigations: conservative initial sampling, closed-loop calibration, and automatic fallbacks.

We accept a small steady-state overhead (bounded by sampling budget) in exchange for reduced catastrophic rollbacks that cost more GPU work.
rollout_plan:
1) Canary: enable on 0.5% of traffic for a set of low-risk routes with simple prompt shapes. Collect acceptance and rollback metrics for 48 hours. 2) Ramp: increase to 5% with adaptive sampling enabled; tune calibrator offline. 3) Route expansion: open to higher-traffic routes with per-route caps and safety circuit-breakers. 4) Enterprise opt-in: expose per-customer controls (Dedicated/Private) for customers who want the feature.

Each stage gated by automated SLO checks (latency regressions, rollback rate, GPU util).
test_plan: Unit tests for sampler logic and calibrator. Integration tests for commit-state transitions including failure injection. Stress tests in runtime-staging using replayed production traces to validate rollback reduction and resource bounds. Add e2e scenario in canary to simulate model-serving preemption and verify graceful fallback. CI must run KV cache coherence checks.
